FACILITY DESCRIPTION The Permittee owns and operates a municipal wastewater treatment facility (WWTF) and associated wastewater collection, recycling, and disposal facilities that serve a population of 16,900 residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural and municipal users in the unincorporated town of McKinleyville. 2.1. Description of Wastewater and Biosolids Treatment and Controls The Facility is located to the west of McKinleyville, California, just east of the Mad River and serves the unincorporated town of McKinleyville. Treated wastewater is discharged from Discharge Point 001 to the Mad River when flows in the Mad River exceed 200 cubic feet per second (cfs) as measured at United States Geological Survey (USGS) gauge at Highway 299. During dry weather, effluent is recycled for dry-weather maintenance of the Hiller storm water treatment wetland, the adjacent forested area, or irrigation of agricultural lands. The Permittee also has the option of recycling effluent through irrigation on the northern portion of the former Fisher parcel north of the railroad bridge, on the lower Fisher Ranch, or on the West Pialorsi Ranch. 2.1.1. Collection System The Permittee’s wastewater collection system consists of approximately 64 miles of gravity sewer mains, 2 miles of pressure force mains, 1,017 sanitary manholes, and 5 pump stations. Gravity sewer lines range in size from 6-inch diameter to 24-inch diameter, but most are 6-inch diameter lines. 2.1.2. Wastewater

chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.citation: Ma, Y et al. (2009). Achieving nitrogen removal via nitrite in a pilot-scale continuous pre-denitrification plant. nan.
chunks.text:
The traditional biological nitrogen removal processes utilized in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) involve the oxidation of ammonium (NH 4 þ ) to nitrate (NO 3 À ) (nitrification) followed by nitrate reduction with an organic carbon source to nitrogen gas (N 2 ) (denitrification). Both nitrification and denitrification possess nitrite (NO 2 À ) as an intermediate. Hence, if

nitrification is stopped at nitrite, denitritation from nitrite to nitrogen gas can be achieved (Verstraete et al., 1977) . Nitrogen removal via nitrite yields 25% reduction in oxygen demand for nitrification and 40% reduction in chemical oxygen demand (COD) requirement for denitrification (Pollice et al., 2002; Turk and Mavinic, 1987) . The reduction in COD requirement would be particularly advantageous for WWTPs treating wastewater with a low COD to nitrogen ratio.

Partial denitrification (PD) refers to the process of controlling NO 3 − -N reduced to NO 2 − -N without further reducing to nitrogen gas (N 2 ).

chunks.text: This study deals with wastewater treatment on a pilot-scale plant set up by electrochemical technology. The electrocoagulation and electroflocculation techniques were applied with a revived design to meet the needs of the process to remove suspended solids and micropollutants out of the wastewater stream. By using various settings of applied currents, the process was tested for the better quality of effluent using water from the outflow of primary sedimentation tank and treated water from the outflow of secondary sedimentation tank. Furthermore, the results are optimized for a better downstream separation process. Wastewater from primary sedimentation tank was treated with both Fe and Al electrodes. In the case of Fe electrodes, more than 50 % of COD removal was observed which was about 12-18 % with Al electrodes. The coagulation dose of Fe and Al electrodes were measured, on the basis of AFS produced and according to Faraday's Law. With both Fe and Al electrodes, the coagulation dose went on increasing with increasing current density.

chunks.text: Electrochemical treatment systems have been shown to provide effective treatment of latrine wastewater. Greater than 5-log inactivation of bacterial and viral indicator organisms is achieved via production of reactive chlorine species from chloride (15−20 mM) within 1 h at 4 V applied cell potential. 3 A combination of reactive chlorine species and direct oxidation provide reduction of chemical oxygen demand (COD) 4 and transformation of trace organic contaminants within 4 h (3.5− 4.5 V applied cell potential) 5−7 with rates enhanced at elevated chloride concentrations (up to 75 mM). Under similar operating conditions, ammonium removal occurs via breakpoint chlorination, 8 and phosphorus can be precipitated as hydroxyapatite. 9 Unfortunately, strongly oxidizing conditions in the presence of the high concentrations of chloride and organic matter typical of latrine wastewater also result in formation of toxic byproducts. 10 While wastewater disinfection is essential to protecting human health, an ideal electrochemical system should also be designed to minimize toxic byproduct formation. 11 Chloride enhances electrochemical treatment via formation of reactive chlorine species (e.g., hypochlorous acid, chloramines, and chlorine radicals).

Monthly average effluent limits from the WRRF are cBOD of 13 mg/L, TSS of 30 mg/L, and ammonia nitrogen limits of 4.1 mg/L. Effluent is discharged to the Canadian River in the Arkansas River watershed. The Norman WRRF provides seasonal reuse to the University of Oklahoma for irrigation of the Jimmie Austin Golf Course. chunks.text: In the activated sludge process the majority of biological solids removed in the secondary sedimentation tank are recycled (returned sludge). The feedback of most of the cell yields from the sedimentation tank encourages rapid adsorption of the pollutants in the incoming settled sewage and also serves to stabilize the operation over a wide range of dilution rates and substrate concentrations imposed by fluctuations in the flow and strength of the wastewater. Secondary treatment processes can remove up to 95 per cent of the BOD and suspended solids entering the process, as well as significant amounts of heavy metals and certain organic compounds which could otherwise cause the deterioration of chemical and ecological quality of receiving waters [10, 53] . Conventional wastewater treatment usually ends with secondary treatment which cannot efficiently remove all the different compounds found in sewage and therefore treated effluents are one of the main sources of persistent micropollutants in the environment [1, 62] . For water reuse, tertiary treatment is needed to provide additional removal of contaminants such as microbial pathogens, particulates, or nutrients, and advanced treatment processes are employed when wastewater is to be reclaimed for reuse, depending on the type of use and quality requirements [49] .

chunks.citation: Kim, T et al. (2021). Dissolved oxygen concentrations affect the function but not the relative abundance of nitrifying bacterial populations in full-scale municipal wastewater treatment bioreactors during cold weather. nan.
chunks.text: The municipal wastewater treatment process reduces contaminants (organic matter, nitrogen, phosphorus, toxic chemicals, and pathogens) in wastewater before its discharge to natural water bodies. Untreated municipal wastewater typically contains 10-50 mg/ L of organic nitrogen (as N), which is converted to ammonia via ammonification during treatment (Tchobanoglous et al., 2003) . This ammonia then poses a substantial risk to surface water quality because of its toxicity to aquatic fauna, contribution to eutrophication (particularly in coastal areas), and concomitant consumption of oxygen during nitrification (Tchobanoglous et al., 2003) . Numerous municipal wastewater treatment facilities, therefore, are designed to perform nitrification to ameliorate the environmental concerns posed by ammonia. Canonical nitrification involves two distinct bacterial populations to oxidize ammonia to nitrate (Brock, 1999) . Ammonia oxidizing bacteria (AOB) oxidize ammonia first to hydroxylamine and then to nitrite. Nitrite oxidizing bacteria (NOB) then oxidize nitrite to nitrate.
